title: Routes, HTTP Methods, and Status Codes
summary: Map methods and paths to handlers, use GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE the way clients expect, and answer with the right status code.
intro: Roombook answers one request so far. A real API answers dozens: list the rooms, show one, book it, change the booking, cancel it. Each needs a route, the right HTTP method, and the right status code, and clients rely on all three. A browser retries a GET without asking, a phone app retries a POST on a bad connection, and a client's code checks the status before it reads a word of the body. This lesson builds Roombook's routes for rooms and bookings with Express routers, then goes through the methods one by one, GET and HEAD, POST, PUT and PATCH, and DELETE, and ends with a map of every status code the API sends and when.

steps.title: Routes and path parameters

examples.title: A room that exists
examples.prompt: With `npm run dev` running, read room 1.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 99
ETag: W/"63-NSrfY7GWv7SId8XCn7/vZtgopSo"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:56:52 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

{"id":1,"name":"Turing","building":"main-library","capacity":6,"amenities":["whiteboard","screen"]}
examples.explanation: The request matched `GET /v1/rooms/:roomId`, so Express called that handler with `req.params.roomId` set to `"1"`. `parseId` turned it into the number 1, and the handler found room 1, Turing, and sent it with `res.json`. The JSON is the same room you met at the start of the course: its id, its name, its building's slug, how many people fit, and its amenities. Notice that `id` is the number 1, while `roomId` was the text `"1"`: the one in the body came from Roombook's own data, not from the path.

examples.title: An id that isn't a number
examples.prompt: Ask for a room whose id is text.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 39
ETag: W/"27-KDHzNLtBGF1z0KTTANqO8h4lzjg"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:56:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

{"status":404,"title":"Room not found"}
examples.explanation: The path matched `/v1/rooms/:roomId` with `roomId` set to `"abc"`, but `parseId` returned `undefined`, so the handler answered 404 with the first-draft error body. A request for `/v1/rooms/99`, a valid id with no room, gets exactly the same answer, down to the `ETag`, since the body is the same. The `status` in the body repeats the status line, which helps when a body travels without its headers, like in a log. Later lessons add the `type`, `detail`, and `instance` fields that say more about what went wrong.

examples.title: A method the path doesn't support
examples.prompt: `-X POST` makes curl send POST instead of GET.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Allow: GET, HEAD, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 43
ETag: W/"2b-kKWwaDleZo9l9WjzXsKNyjiMHGg"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:56:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

{"status":405,"title":"Method Not Allowed"}
examples.explanation: The path `/v1/rooms/1` matched, but the route has no POST handler, so the request fell through to `.all(methodNotAllowed(...))`. The `Allow` header tells the client which methods would have worked, and a developer can read it to see their mistake: to create a room, you POST to `/v1/rooms`, not to one room's address. Without the `.all` line, Express would have answered `404 Not Found` with an HTML page saying `Cannot POST /v1/rooms/1`, which wrongly suggests that room 1 doesn't exist.

steps.title: GET and HEAD: reading

examples.title: Every room
examples.prompt: Without `-i`, curl prints only the body.
examples.explanation: All three rooms come back inside `items`, in the order the `Map` holds them, which is the order they were added. Express writes JSON with no spaces or line breaks, the smallest form, which is right for programs and hard for people. To read it comfortably, open the same address in a browser, since Firefox and Chrome both lay JSON out neatly, and the lesson on curl, Postman, and OpenAPI shows jq, the terminal tool most developers use for this.

examples.title: HEAD for the same room
examples.prompt: `-I` sends HEAD and prints the headers it gets back.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 99
ETag: W/"63-NSrfY7GWv7SId8XCn7/vZtgopSo"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:56:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
examples.explanation: The status and headers match the GET for room 1 exactly, down to `Content-Length: 99` and the `ETag`, but no body came back. Express ran the GET handler, which built the whole response, then sent only its head. That's useful to a client that only needs to know whether room 1 exists, or whether its saved copy is still current: it compares the `ETag` with the one it kept, without paying for the body.

steps.title: POST: creating and actions

examples.title: Creating a room
examples.prompt: `--json` sends its text as the body of a POST, and sets `Content-Type: application/json` for you.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/rooms/4
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 92
ETag: W/"5c-iFJT8Xu1YKuagcn7szwJpUXX500"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:56:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

{"id":4,"name":"Hamilton","building":"science-library","capacity":10,"amenities":["screen"]}
examples.explanation: The repository gave the new room the next id, 4, and the handler answered 201 with `Location: /v1/rooms/4` and the room itself. The single quotes around the JSON keep the terminal from reading its double quotes and brackets as part of the command. `Location` holds a path, not a full URL, which HTTP allows: the client combines it with the address it called. Run the command again and you get room 5, an identical second room, which is the non-idempotent POST in action.

examples.title: Cancelling a booking
examples.prompt: Booking 1001 is Ada's Algorithms study group in Turing, on Monday 5 October 2026.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 213
ETag: W/"d5-LdwVikvUbZPFTHlAMfH0IISTDBg"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:56:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

{"id":1001,"roomId":1,"userId":1,"startsAt":"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z","endsAt":"2026-10-05T15:30:00Z","attendees":3,"note":"Algorithms study group","status":"cancelled","version":2,"createdAt":"2026-10-01T09:00:00Z"}
examples.explanation: The action sent no body, since the path says everything: which booking, and what to do. The answer is 200 with the booking, now `"status":"cancelled"` at `"version":2`. Run it a second time and the answer is the same 200 and the same body, still version 2, since the handler returns a cancelled booking without saving it again. The rules that belong here, like refusing once the booking has started, come in later lessons, when Roombook knows who's asking and what time it is.

steps.title: PUT and PATCH: updating

examples.title: Replacing room 4
examples.prompt: Room 4 is the Hamilton room the POST created. This PUT sends all four fields, with a new capacity and a new amenity.
examples.explanation: `-X PUT` changes the method `--json` would use, which is POST, and keeps the JSON body and its `Content-Type`. The room now holds exactly what the body said: capacity 12, and both amenities. The id is still 4, because it came from the path, not the body. If the server restarted since the POST, room 4 is gone, since the rooms live in memory, and the answer is 404: run the POST from the previous part again first.

examples.title: Patching one field
examples.prompt: `-H` sets a header, here the merge patch's own `Content-Type`, and `-d` sends the body.
examples.explanation: Only the capacity changed, to 8. The name, the building, and both amenities stayed as the PUT left them, since the patch didn't mention them. `-d` alone would send `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, the type an HTML form uses, and `express.json` would ignore the body. Setting the header with `-H` tells Roombook it's a merge patch, which the `type` list in `app.ts` accepts.

examples.title: A PUT that leaves fields out
examples.prompt: The same room, replaced with a body that has only a name.
examples.explanation: The room lost its building, its capacity, and its amenities. The handler did what PUT promises and stored exactly what it got, and the missing fields were `undefined`, which JSON leaves out. This is the classic PUT mistake: a client meant to rename the room and sent only the name. The fix is on both sides. Clients use PATCH to change some fields, and the API rejects a PUT that's missing required fields, which the lesson on validation and errors adds with a 422 that names each missing one.

steps.title: DELETE and what each method promises
steps.body:
Deleting is the change you can't take back, and it's also one that clients retry a lot, since a delete that timed out leaves them unsure whether it happened. So it needs an answer that's clear the first time and safe the second.

## 204 No Content

`DELETE /v1/rooms/:roomId` removes the room and answers **204 No Content**: it worked, and there's nothing to send back.

```ts sketch
.delete((req, res) => {
  const room = rooms.findById(parseId(req.params.roomId));
  if (!room) {
    res.status(404).json({ status: 404, title: "Room not found" });
    return;
  }
  rooms.remove(room.id);
  res.status(204).end();
})
```

A 204 can't have a body, so `res.status(204).end()` sends the status and the headers and stops.

## Soft delete

In memory, Roombook simply removes the room. With a database, it won't. Bookings point at their room, and a booking from last month must still be able to say it was in Turing, so erasing the room would break its history. Instead, Roombook does a **soft delete**: it keeps the room and marks it inactive, and every read skips inactive rooms. To clients, it's gone. To the records, it's still there. The raw SQL lesson adds the `active` column that does this.

Deleting has a rule too: a room with upcoming bookings can't be deleted, because the students who booked it would show up to a room that no longer exists in the system. That gets **409 Conflict**, the code for a request that clashes with the current state of the data, which the lesson on validation and errors explains.

## The second DELETE

After the first DELETE, the room is gone. What should a second, identical DELETE answer? There are two sound choices:

- **204 again**: the client wanted the room gone, and it is.
- **404**: there's no room there to delete.

Either keeps DELETE idempotent, because idempotent means the server ends up in the same state, not that the answer is the same. Roombook answers 404, since nothing is there, and its clients treat a 404 from a DELETE as done. What matters is choosing one and answering it every time, so client developers can rely on it.

## What each method promises

Here's every method Roombook uses, and the promises clients build on:

| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Request body | Cacheable |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GET | yes | yes | no | yes |
| HEAD | yes | yes | no | yes |
| POST | no | no | yes | rarely |
| PUT | no | yes | yes | no |
| PATCH | no | no | yes | no |
| DELETE | no | yes | no | no |
| OPTIONS | yes | yes | no | no |

- **Safe** methods change nothing, so anything may send them at any time.
- **Idempotent** methods can be retried after a timeout without doing the work twice. A client library may retry GET, PUT, and DELETE by itself, but never POST.
- **Request body** says whether the method carries one. A GET or DELETE with a body is allowed by the rules but has no agreed meaning, and many proxies and libraries drop it, so never design an API that needs one.
- **Cacheable** responses may be stored and reused by browsers and caches, which is how a second visit gets faster. A POST answer can only be reused in rare cases most caches ignore.

## OPTIONS

**OPTIONS** asks a server which methods a path supports, and the answer's `Allow` header lists them. Roombook's `methodNotAllowed` answers it with 204 and the list, as the third example shows. Browsers send OPTIONS on their own before some requests from other origins, the CORS preflight from the web course. The security lesson sets up the answers those need.

examples.title: Deleting room 4
examples.prompt: Room 4 must exist, so run the POST that creates it first if the server restarted.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:56:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
examples.explanation: The answer is only a status line and three headers: no `Content-Type`, no `Content-Length`, and no body, since a 204 has none. There's no `ETag` either, as there's no body to fingerprint. Everything a client needs is in the status: the room is deleted. `GET /v1/rooms` no longer lists it, and its id isn't reused, since the repository's counter only goes up. Reusing ids would let an old link to room 4 point at a different room.

examples.title: Deleting it again
examples.prompt: The same command, run a second time.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 39
ETag: W/"27-KDHzNLtBGF1z0KTTANqO8h4lzjg"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:56:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

{"status":404,"title":"Room not found"}
examples.explanation: The handler found no room 4, so it answered 404 before reaching the delete. The server's state is the same as after the first DELETE, which is what makes the method idempotent, even though the status differs. A client that sent the first DELETE, lost the answer, and retried, sees this 404 and knows its goal is met: the room is gone either way.

examples.title: Asking which methods work
examples.prompt: `-X OPTIONS` sends an OPTIONS request for room 1.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Allow: GET, HEAD, PUT, PATCH, DELETE
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:56:53 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
examples.explanation: No route on `/:roomId` has an OPTIONS handler, so the request reached `.all(methodNotAllowed(...))`, which answers OPTIONS with 204 and the `Allow` list instead of an error. The list matches the 405 answer from the first part, since both come from the same string. Keeping that string next to the routes it describes is what keeps them in step: when you add a method to the route, you add it to the list on the line below.

steps.title: Status codes: the full map
steps.body:
The status code is the first thing a client's code reads, before a single byte of the body. It decides what happens next: show the data, show an error, retry, send the user to log in, or give up. An API that picks its codes carefully lets every client handle every answer correctly without parsing error messages.

## The questions, in order

When a request comes in, an API answers a series of questions, and the first one that fails picks the code. Each later lesson builds one of these checks, but the order already tells you which code to send:

```diagram routes-and-methods-status-codes
Each no leads to its code, and the first one that applies wins.
```

## Every code Roombook sends

| Code | Roombook sends it when |
|---|---|
| 200 OK | a read, an update, or an action worked |
| 201 Created | a POST made a room or a booking |
| 202 Accepted | work was queued, to finish later |
| 204 No Content | a DELETE worked |
| 304 Not Modified | the client's saved copy is still current |
| 400 Bad Request | the request can't be read, like broken JSON |
| 401 Unauthorized | there's no valid login, token, or key |
| 403 Forbidden | the caller is known, but not allowed |
| 404 Not Found | no route matches, or no such room or booking |
| 405 Method Not Allowed | the path exists, but not with that method |
| 409 Conflict | the room is already booked at that time |
| 412 Precondition Failed | an `If-Match` header names an old version |
| 413 Content Too Large | the body is over the size limit |
| 415 Unsupported Media Type | the body isn't JSON |
| 422 Unprocessable Content | the JSON is fine, but a value breaks a rule |
| 429 Too Many Requests | the caller is over its rate limit |
| 500 Internal Server Error | a bug, or a crash |
| 502 Bad Gateway | a service Roombook called gave a broken answer |
| 503 Service Unavailable | Roombook is overloaded, or shutting down |
| 504 Gateway Timeout | a service Roombook called didn't answer in time |

Node.js prints a few of these with older names, like `413 Payload Too Large` and `422 Unprocessable Entity`. Only the number counts, and the table uses today's names.

## Pairs that people mix up

- **401 or 403.** 401 means we don't know who you are: log in, or send a valid token. 403 means we know exactly who you are, and you still can't do this, like a member creating a room, which only staff may do.
- **400 or 422.** 400 means the request can't be read at all, like JSON with a missing bracket. 422 means it was read fine, and a value breaks a rule, like booking a room for 6 with 40 attendees.
- **409 or 412.** 409 means the request clashes with the data as it is, like booking a slot that's taken. 412 means the client made its request conditional on a version, with `If-Match`, and the data has changed since it looked, so the server refused to apply a change based on an old copy.

## 4xx or 5xx: who must act

A **4xx** means the client must change something. Sending the same request again gets the same answer, so a client shouldn't retry it as it is. Two are exceptions worth knowing: after a 429, a client waits as long as the `Retry-After` header says and tries again, and after a 409, it can read the latest data and then decide.

A **5xx** means the server failed, and the request itself may have been fine. A retry a little later may work, especially after a 502, 503, or 504. But only retry what's safe to repeat: a GET, a PUT, a DELETE, or a POST with an idempotency key, from the lesson on retries and idempotency. Retrying a plain POST after a 504 can book a room twice, since the first request may have worked before the answer was lost.

## Never 200 for an error

Some APIs answer every request with 200, and put `{"error": "..."}` in the body. Don't. Caches store a 200 and hand the error to the next person, monitoring counts it as a success, and every client has to read the body to find out that something went wrong. In Express, `res.status(code)` sets the code before you send the body with `res.json`, as the 404 and 405 handlers do. Their bodies are a first draft: the middleware lesson sends every error through one place, and the lesson on validation and errors gives them the full Problem Details format.

The next lesson reads the rest of a request: its query string, its headers, and its body.

recap:
- A route is a method plus a path pattern, like GET /v1/rooms/:roomId, and Express runs the first one that matches.
- Path parameters arrive as strings in req.params, and an id that isn't valid gets 404, like one that doesn't exist.
- A known path with the wrong method gets 405 with an Allow header, and Express needs .all() to send it.
- GET and HEAD only read, so crawlers, caches, and retries can send them at any time.
- POST creates with 201 and a Location header, runs actions like cancel, and isn't safe to repeat.
- PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent, and PATCH with JSON Merge Patch changes only the fields it sends.
- DELETE answers 204, Roombook soft-deletes rooms, and a second DELETE gets 404 every time.
- 4xx means the client must change the request, 5xx means the server failed, and an error never gets 200.
